definition: Cryptographic schemes designed to remain secure against adversaries with large-scale quantum computers, usually built on lattices, hash functions, codes, or other structures for which no efficient quantum attack is known.

An adversary records quantum-vulnerable ciphertext today and retains it until a sufficiently capable quantum computer is available. The relevant deadline depends on the data's confidentiality lifetime, not only on when such a computer appears.

A model-based estimate of the logical qubits, physical qubits, gate count, runtime and error-correction overhead required by a quantum attack. Estimates depend strongly on hardware, noise and code assumptions and are not arrival-date predictions.

A quantum algorithm that factors integers and computes discrete logarithms in polynomial time, breaking RSA, finite-field Diffie–Hellman, and elliptic-curve cryptography once a sufficiently large fault-tolerant quantum computer exists.

A quantum search algorithm giving a quadratic speed-up for unstructured search, including symmetric key and hash-preimage search. Quantum collision search uses different algorithms and cost exponents, so it should not be described as a generic Grover speed-up.
A coarse comparison point used by NIST PQC standards: category 1 is roughly as hard as key search on AES-128, while category 5 is roughly as hard as key search on AES-256.
A named collection of sizes and constants for a cryptographic scheme (for example ML-KEM-768). Parameter sets trade security, ciphertext or signature size, and computational cost.
Encryption in which anyone can encrypt with a public key while only the holder of the matching secret key can decrypt.
A primitive that binds a message to a secret key so that anyone with the corresponding public key can verify authenticity and integrity, and the signer cannot credibly deny signing.

A three-algorithm interface — KeyGen, Encaps, Decaps — that establishes a shared secret. Encapsulation takes a public key and returns a ciphertext plus a session key; decapsulation recovers that key from the secret key and ciphertext.
The symmetric part of a hybrid encryption construction, typically an AEAD scheme that encrypts application data under a freshly encapsulated key.
Indistinguishability under adaptive chosen-ciphertext attack. The adversary may query a decryption oracle even after seeing the challenge ciphertext, but may not decrypt that exact ciphertext.

A generic construction that converts a weakly secure public-key encryption or KEM scheme into an IND-CCA2-secure KEM, typically by deriving randomness from the message and re-encrypting during decapsulation to check consistency.

The event in which noise and rounding cause a KEM to recover a different message than the one encapsulated. In ML-KEM this is made vanishingly rare by parameter choice and is implicitly rejected by the FO re-encryption check.

Lossy rounding that drops low-order bits from lattice coefficients before transmission, shrinking ciphertexts. Decompression reconstructs an approximation; correctness must tolerate the induced error.
The problem of recovering a secret vector from noisy linear equations over a finite field. Its conjectured worst-case hardness underlies many lattice-based post-quantum schemes.
An LWE variant over modules of polynomial rings. It sits between unstructured LWE and ring-LWE, giving a tunable balance between security confidence, key size, and speed.
An LWE variant over a polynomial quotient ring such as Z_q[X]/(X^n + 1), enabling compact keys and fast multiplication via the NTT.
The quotient ring R_q = Z_q[X]/(X^n + 1). Multiplying two degree-(n-1) polynomials wraps high-degree terms around with a sign flip, which makes the ring compatible with negacyclic NTTs.
A finite-field analogue of the Fourier transform that multiplies polynomials in O(n log n) instead of O(n^2). ML-KEM uses a negacyclic NTT over Z_3329 with 128 butterflies.
The basic NTT/FFT computation combining two coefficients with a twiddle factor. A layer of independent butterflies transforms an array in place.
Mapping an integer back into a bounded representative modulo q. Cryptography uses branch-free variants such as Barrett and Montgomery reduction to avoid secret-dependent timing.

A technique for computing modular multiplication without division by q, using a precomputed constant and shifts. Widely used in lattice and elliptic-curve implementations because it is fast and easy to make constant-time.
A distribution-shaping technique that outputs a candidate only if it passes a bound or acceptance test. Lattice signatures use it so that signatures reveal nothing useful about the secret key.
A signature built only from hash functions, giving conservative security assumptions at the cost of larger signatures and, for some schemes, state management.
Winternitz One-Time Signature Plus: a hash-based one-time signature that signs base-w digits by revealing hash chains. A single key pair must never sign two different messages.
Forest of Random Subsets: a few-time hash-based signature used in SPHINCS+ to sign a digest by revealing one secret leaf per tree in a small forest.
A tree of Merkle trees used by SLH-DSA to extend a small number of one-time keys into many stateless signatures. Each layer signs the roots of trees below it.
eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme, a stateful hash-based signature standardized in RFC 8391. It is efficient but requires the signer to track which one-time keys have been used.

Writing code whose control flow and memory-access pattern do not depend on secret data, so timing and cache observations do not leak secrets. It is a necessary but not sufficient defence against all physical side channels.
An attack that exploits physical or implementation leakage — time, power, cache state, electromagnetic emanations — rather than breaking the mathematical primitive.
A statistical side-channel attack that correlates many power traces with hypothetical intermediate values to recover secret-dependent information.

A countermeasure that splits secret-dependent values into random shares so that a defined set of shares is independent of the secret under a stated probing model. Boolean and arithmetic masking are common building blocks, but composability, glitches and higher-order probes require separate analysis.

A statistical leakage-assessment method that compares trace distributions for fixed-versus-random or specific public-input classes. A non-significant result only bounds detectable leakage under the stated sample size, effect size and test setup; it is not proof that no leakage exists.
An attack that induces hardware faults during computation and observes incorrect outputs to recover secrets. Redundant computation and verification are standard countermeasures.

Combining a classical key agreement (such as X25519) with a post-quantum KEM so that the resulting shared secret is secure if either component remains secure. The selected group fixes component order and encoding; X25519MLKEM768 places ML-KEM first despite its name.
The engineering ability to replace algorithms, parameter sets, and certificate types without redesigning an entire protocol or product. It is a prerequisite for a multi-decade PQC migration.
The certificates, authorities, policies, and revocation mechanisms that bind public keys to identities. PQC migration changes key and signature sizes as well as algorithm identifiers.
A signed data structure binding a subject identity to a public key and extensions. Post-quantum signatures increase certificate sizes and can strain handshake and buffer limits.
The authenticated key exchange that establishes traffic keys for a TLS connection. It negotiates a key-exchange group and authenticates the server (and optionally client) with signatures.
Schemes whose security rests on the difficulty of decoding random or structured linear codes. Classic McEliece is the canonical example, with very large public keys but compact ciphertexts.
A family of algebraic error-correcting codes used by the McEliece cryptosystem. Its efficient decoding structure is hidden by scrambling the generator matrix.
A code-based KEM with a long track record and conservative security, but public keys on the order of a megabyte. It illustrates the PQC design space beyond lattices and hashes.

Schemes based on the difficulty of finding isogenies between elliptic curves. SIKE was a prominent candidate until a 2022 key-recovery attack, a cautionary case study in algorithm diversity and review.
The multi-round public process that selected ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, and additional candidates such as HQC. It produced FIPS 203, 204, and 205 in August 2024.
An encryption interface that provides confidentiality plus integrity and authenticity for ciphertext and associated data, returning a single failure on tampering.
A value that must be unique for each encryption under a given key. Nonce reuse can break confidentiality and authentication, especially in GCM and stream ciphers.
An AEAD mode combining counter-mode encryption with GHASH authentication. It requires unique nonces and a careful key lifecycle.
A stream-cipher AEAD combining ChaCha20 encryption with Poly1305 authentication, popular in software and on devices without AES acceleration.
The lifecycle of cryptographic keys: generation, distribution, storage, rotation, revocation, recovery and destruction.
A keyed message authentication code built from a hash function with inner and outer pads, avoiding the length-extension weakness of secret-prefix hashing.
An extract-and-expand key derivation function that turns input keying material into one or more purpose-specific keys with explicit context binding.
A memory-hard password-hashing function designed to make offline guessing expensive and resist some side-channel and GPU attacks.
Storing a salted, deliberately expensive derivation of a password so that verification is possible but fast offline guessing is not.
A weakness of some Merkle–Damgård hash constructions that lets an attacker extend a message and recompute a valid digest when the secret is used as a prefix. HMAC avoids this.
Concentrating authority, state or control in one operator. It enables fast coordination and recovery, but creates censorship, availability and breach concentration risks.
Distributing authority among multiple participants. It can improve censorship resistance and resilience but adds coordination, governance and consensus costs.
A fault where a participant behaves arbitrarily or maliciously, including sending conflicting messages, rather than simply stopping.
The result that a distributed data store cannot simultaneously guarantee strong consistency, availability and partition tolerance; under a partition it must trade one off.
A protocol that lets distributed participants agree on an ordered sequence of values despite crashes, delays or malicious behaviour.
A security architecture that removes implicit trust based on network location and authenticates and authorises every request.
Training a shared model across distributed clients that keep their raw data local and share model updates instead.
A protocol that lets a server compute the sum of client updates without seeing any individual update. It protects confidentiality, not correctness.
A formal privacy guarantee bounding the influence of any single record on the output of a randomised computation.
An attack that determines whether a specific record was used to train a model, exploiting memorisation or confidence differences.
An attack in which a participant submits a malicious update to degrade a shared model or install a backdoor. Secure aggregation does not prevent it.
Inspection of protocol fields and payloads beyond basic headers, used for intrusion detection, application control and policy enforcement.
Analysing metadata about network conversations — endpoints, ports, bytes, packets, timing — rather than payload content. It remains useful when traffic is encrypted.
An intrusion detection system alerts on suspicious traffic; an intrusion prevention system sits inline and can block it. Inline blocking raises false-positive impact.
Terminating TLS at a proxy to inspect plaintext. It creates a high-value key and trust target, breaks end-to-end guarantees and raises legal and privacy issues.
The team and system that monitor telemetry, detect and triage security events, coordinate incident response and improve detections.
Security information and event management: a platform that collects, normalises, correlates and searches security telemetry.
Designing, testing, deploying and maintaining detections as versioned products with owners, data dependencies, precision targets and runbooks.
The degradation of analyst judgement caused by excessive, low-quality alerts. It is a security failure, not merely an operational inconvenience.
The structured process of preparing for, detecting, containing, eradicating, recovering from and learning from security incidents.
A knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques used to map detection coverage, structure threat hunting and communicate about behaviour.
A vendor-neutral format for describing SIEM detections that can be converted into multiple query languages.
A hypothesis-driven search for adversary activity that existing detections may have missed, using telemetry and threat intelligence.
A proof that convinces a verifier of a statement without revealing the witness, satisfying completeness, soundness and zero knowledge.
An interactive proof of knowledge of a discrete logarithm using a commitment, challenge and response; Fiat–Shamir makes it non-interactive.
A succinct non-interactive argument of knowledge. Many constructions offer tiny proofs but rely on a trusted setup and non-standard assumptions.
Protocols that let parties compute a function over private inputs while revealing only the result, under a specified corruption and network model.
Splitting a secret into shares so that a qualified subset can reconstruct it while any smaller subset reveals nothing. Shamir's scheme is the classic threshold construction.
A parameter-generation ceremony for some proof systems. If the secret randomness is retained or compromised, soundness or zero knowledge can fail.
An authorised adversarial exercise that tests detection, response and resilience using scoped techniques and evidence-backed findings.
Written scope, targets, techniques, stop conditions, escalation contacts and evidence requirements that authorise and bound a security test.
A vulnerability in which untrusted input changes the structure of a database query, allowing unauthorised reading or modification.
A vulnerability in which attacker-controlled content executes in another user's browser under a trusted origin.
An attack that causes a browser to send an authenticated request the user did not intend, exploiting ambient credentials.
A vulnerability in which an attacker makes a server issue requests to unintended destinations, often reaching internal services or metadata endpoints.
An authorisation framework that lets a client obtain scoped access to a protected resource without sharing the resource owner's credentials.
An identity layer on OAuth 2.0 that adds authentication and standard identity claims through ID tokens.
A web authentication standard using public-key credentials and an authenticator ceremony to resist phishing and shared-secret theft.
A machine-readable inventory of components, dependencies and related metadata in a software artifact.
Verifiable evidence describing where an artifact came from, which source and build process produced it, and what inputs influenced it.
A framework for progressively improving build integrity through source, build and provenance security levels.
Malware or a mechanism that hides its presence or alters system views at user, kernel or firmware layers.
Persistence that modifies the boot process, bootloader or firmware so malicious code executes before normal security controls are fully active.
The firmware interface that initialises hardware and starts the bootloader and operating system; it forms an early trust boundary.
A firmware verification mechanism that allows only trusted, correctly signed boot components to execute.
Analysis of volatile RAM to identify processes, injected code, network artefacts, credentials and other evidence that may disappear on shutdown.
Analysis of file-system structures and metadata to reconstruct file activity, recover deleted records and validate evidence.
A correlated chronological view combining events from multiple sources after normalising clocks and documenting uncertainty.
The documented history of evidence collection, hashing, handling, storage and transfer so its integrity can be demonstrated.
